title: Outdoor Cultivation
purpose: Expand the Outdoor Cultivation subject into a systems curriculum covering site selection, seasonal light, acclimation, transplant establishment, root-zone water, structural support, flower-weather risk, pest and wildlife controls, pollen drift, microclimates, contingencies and records.
learningOutcome: A learner should be able to evaluate an outdoor site from seasonal sun, drainage, water access, airflow, terrain and neighboring risks; acclimate and transplant plants without treating hardening as a fixed calendar recipe; distinguish rainfall from actual root-zone water status; design support for wind and branch load; interpret flower microclimates and rain-related disease pressure; build scouting and wildlife controls around prevention; manage sex expression and pollen-drift risk without claiming one fixed zero-risk isolation distance; and use local weather, microclimate observations and season records to improve future crop planning.
evidenceBoundary: Cannabis-specific field and plant-pathology evidence is used for pollen, flower microclimates and disease where available. University horticulture guidance is used only for transferable principles such as hardening, transplant establishment and staking. Numeric isolation distances, irrigation volumes and seasonal dates are not presented as universal.

chapters.title: Site Selection & Seasonal Sun
chapters.objective: Choose a site from measured seasonal exposure, drainage, airflow, water access and neighboring risk rather than from a single midday observation.

lessons.title: Map sun over the season, not one afternoon
lessons.summary: Solar angle, day length, trees, buildings and terrain change direct-light duration through the season, so a site should be observed or modeled across the intended crop period.
lessons.cultivation: A location that looks open in spring can develop long summer or autumn shadows as sun angle and vegetation change.
lessons.observe: Record direct-sun windows at several dates or use a sun-path tool and verify obstacles from the actual plant position.

lessons.title: Drainage and topography shape the root environment
lessons.summary: Slope, soil structure, compaction, low spots and raised beds or containers determine whether rainfall drains, ponds or moves away from roots.
lessons.cultivation: A sunny site can still fail if the root zone remains saturated after storms or if runoff erodes the planting area.
lessons.observe: Inspect the site after real rainfall and note ponding duration, runoff paths, erosion and soil structure rather than guessing from dry soil.

lessons.title: Water access is a design constraint
lessons.summary: Outdoor irrigation depends on source reliability, pressure or pumping, hose/line length, filtration needs and the ability to deliver water evenly during peak demand.
lessons.cultivation: A remote site with strong sun but unreliable water can create preventable stress and emergency watering practices.
lessons.observe: Test the source and delivery system before planting and record flow or distribution problems at the farthest points.

lessons.title: Neighboring land can create biological and environmental risk
lessons.summary: Nearby hemp/cannabis pollen sources, dusty roads, spray drift, standing water, unmanaged vegetation, lighting or human access can change site suitability.
lessons.cultivation: Site selection includes what can move into the crop by wind, water, animals and people.
lessons.observe: Walk the surrounding area, identify likely upwind sources and revisit the risk map as neighboring crops and seasonal winds change.

knowledgeChecks: Why is a single midday sun check insufficient for site selection?
What should be observed after rainfall before judging drainage?
Which water-delivery constraints should be tested before planting?
What neighboring sources can create risk even when the planting area itself looks suitable?

chapters.title: Hardening Off & Transplant Establishment
chapters.objective: Move plants outdoors gradually and establish roots with repeatable observations instead of a fixed hardening calendar.

lessons.title: Hardening is gradual acclimation to multiple stresses
lessons.summary: Protected plants must adjust to brighter sunlight, wind, larger temperature swings and different humidity; exposure should increase based on plant response and weather rather than a universal day count.
lessons.cultivation: A plant adapted to indoor light can scorch or wilt outdoors even when air temperature seems mild.
lessons.observe: Increase exposure in steps and inspect leaf angle, color, turgor, surface damage and recovery before the next increase.

lessons.title: Use weather windows to reduce transplant shock
lessons.summary: Extreme heat, cold, strong wind or intense midday radiation increases demand during a period when disturbed roots may not yet supply water normally.
lessons.cultivation: Transplant timing should reflect actual forecast and site conditions rather than only plant age.
lessons.observe: Record forecast, soil/root-zone moisture, wind and sunlight around transplant and compare recovery across different conditions.

lessons.title: Protect root-ball integrity and planting depth
lessons.summary: Handle the root ball with minimal tearing, avoid burying stems or crowns inappropriately, remove constricting containers and backfill without creating large air gaps.
lessons.cultivation: Severe root disturbance or poor contact between root ball and surrounding media can delay water uptake.
lessons.observe: Inspect roots before planting, document circling or damaged roots and check whether irrigation wets both the root ball and surrounding soil.

lessons.title: Establishment is a monitored transition
lessons.summary: The first days after transplant should be evaluated from turgor, new growth, root-zone moisture and weather response rather than assumed successful after one watering.
lessons.cultivation: Plants can appear acceptable in cool weather and show establishment problems during the first high-demand period.
lessons.observe: Check at comparable times of day and distinguish temporary midday wilt from persistent loss of turgor or stalled growth.

knowledgeChecks: Why is hardening better managed from plant response than a fixed number of days?
Which weather conditions can increase transplant stress?
Why must irrigation reach both the original root ball and surrounding soil?
What observations show that establishment is progressing?

chapters.title: Outdoor Water, Irrigation & Root-Zone Balance
chapters.objective: Manage root-zone water from measured soil/media conditions, rainfall, drainage and plant demand rather than from rainfall totals or a rigid schedule alone.

lessons.title: Rainfall is input, not proof of root-zone recharge
lessons.summary: Canopy interception, runoff, slope, mulch, soil texture and rain intensity determine how much rainfall actually enters the active root zone.
lessons.cultivation: A recorded storm can leave container media or sheltered root zones surprisingly dry, while another storm can saturate low ground.
lessons.observe: Check moisture at root depth after representative rain events instead of subtracting rainfall totals mechanically from irrigation.

lessons.title: Irrigation should wet the intended root volume
lessons.summary: Application rate, emitter placement, soil infiltration and root spread determine whether water reaches a useful volume or creates isolated wet spots.
lessons.cultivation: Large outdoor plants can outgrow an early-season watering footprint and develop dry outer root zones.
lessons.observe: Periodically excavate or probe carefully at several distances/depths and verify distribution rather than assuming runtime equals coverage.

lessons.title: Mulch changes evaporation and temperature
lessons.summary: Mulch can reduce surface evaporation and buffer soil temperature, but thick wet mulch against the stem can also change moisture and disease conditions.
lessons.cultivation: Mulch modifies the water balance, so irrigation frequency may need to change after it is added.
lessons.observe: Compare under-mulch moisture and temperature with unmulched reference areas and keep material appropriately clear of the stem base.

lessons.title: Drainage and salinity still matter outdoors
lessons.summary: Repeated irrigation, fertilizer inputs, low-quality source water or restricted drainage can create salt accumulation or oxygen-limited roots despite outdoor rainfall.
lessons.cultivation: Outdoor growing does not eliminate root-zone chemistry or aeration constraints.
lessons.observe: Use source-water measurements, root-zone observations and runoff/leachate context where appropriate before diagnosing foliage symptoms as nutrient deficiency.

knowledgeChecks: Why is rainfall total not the same as root-zone recharge?
How can a plant outgrow its irrigation wetting pattern?
What changes should be expected after adding mulch?
Why can salinity and poor aeration remain outdoor problems?

chapters.title: Wind, Support & Canopy Architecture
chapters.objective: Design support around prevailing wind, branch leverage and plant growth while preserving movement and avoiding constriction.

lessons.title: Wind load increases with exposed area and leverage
lessons.summary: Large leaves, long branches and heavy flowers create forces that rise with wind speed and distance from the supporting stem or tie point.
lessons.cultivation: A branch that was stable in vegetative growth can fail later when flower mass and storm gusts increase.
lessons.observe: Identify prevailing wind direction, exposed edges and long unsupported branches before severe weather arrives.

lessons.title: Support should distribute load
lessons.summary: Stakes, cages, trellises and lines should spread forces across multiple points rather than concentrating pressure on one stem or tie.
lessons.cultivation: A strong support system can still injure plants if ties cut into expanding stems or rub during wind.
lessons.observe: Use flexible ties, inspect contact points regularly and allow room for stem thickening.

lessons.title: Some movement is normal and informative
lessons.summary: Completely immobilizing every stem is not necessary; the objective is to prevent lodging and breakage while allowing normal movement and growth.
lessons.cultivation: Overbuilt support can hide weak attachment points until load shifts elsewhere.
lessons.observe: After moderate wind, inspect where the plant moved, which ties carried load and whether bark or stems were damaged.

lessons.title: Canopy architecture affects both wind and moisture
lessons.summary: Dense walls of foliage catch wind and can also slow drying after rain; spacing, selective pruning and support geometry alter both risks.
lessons.cultivation: Wind protection and disease prevention should be designed together rather than as opposing one-variable goals.
lessons.observe: Observe how quickly different canopy zones dry after dew or rain and where branches rub or overlap.

knowledgeChecks: Why does branch leverage matter as flowers gain mass?
What makes a support tie damaging?
Why is complete immobilization not the goal?
How can canopy architecture affect both wind load and post-rain drying?

chapters.title: Rain, Humidity & Flower Disease Risk
chapters.objective: Interpret weather risk at the flower microclimate, especially during dense reproductive growth, and use inspection rather than room-style averages.

lessons.title: Flower humidity can exceed ambient humidity
lessons.summary: Dense inflorescences create sheltered internal spaces where transpired water and slow air exchange can produce higher humidity than a nearby weather station reports.
lessons.cultivation: An acceptable ambient RH does not prove the interior of a large flower dried quickly after rain or dew.
lessons.observe: Inspect and, where feasible, measure representative dense flowers rather than relying only on a sensor several meters away.

lessons.title: Cool, wet periods increase Botrytis concern
lessons.summary: Cannabis disease literature consistently identifies prolonged moisture, rain, high humidity and susceptible flower tissue as important Botrytis risk factors.
lessons.cultivation: Risk rises when flowers remain wet or humid for extended periods, especially late in flowering when tissue is dense.
lessons.observe: Track rainfall, dew, drying time, flower density and symptom development together; do not diagnose from weather alone.

lessons.title: Post-rain drying opportunity matters
lessons.summary: Sun, wind, canopy spacing, temperature and subsequent humidity determine how quickly free water and high-humidity pockets dissipate after rain.
lessons.cultivation: Two storms with the same rainfall total can create different disease pressure if one is followed by warm dry wind and the other by cool humid conditions.
lessons.observe: Record when flowers become visibly dry and inspect sheltered zones after repeated wet events.

lessons.title: Triage suspect flowers without spreading contamination
lessons.summary: Discolored, soft, collapsed or mold-suspect tissue should be inspected carefully, segregated as appropriate and handled with clean tools rather than pulled through healthy canopy.
lessons.cultivation: Aggressive handling of suspect rot can spread spores or debris through nearby flowers.
lessons.observe: Photograph symptoms, note location/weather history and clean tools between suspect and healthy material.

chapters.title: Pests, Wildlife & Outdoor Biosecurity
chapters.objective: Use routine scouting, physical exclusion, sanitation and evidence-based diagnosis before reaching for reactive controls.

lessons.title: Scout on a schedule and after disruptive weather
lessons.summary: Outdoor pest and disease pressure changes with season, neighboring vegetation and storms, so scouting should cover repeatable zones and increase after events that move insects or damage tissue.
lessons.cultivation: Only looking after visible damage allows populations or disease to establish before the first record exists.
lessons.observe: Use a fixed route, inspect upper/lower leaf surfaces and flowers as appropriate, and record presence, absence and approximate severity.

lessons.title: Physical exclusion is often the first wildlife layer
lessons.summary: Fencing, netting, guards and site design can reduce deer, rodents, birds or digging damage without relying on unverified repellents.
lessons.cultivation: Wildlife prevention should be designed around the actual animal and failure route rather than a generic deterrent.
lessons.observe: Document tracks, bite patterns, digging, droppings and entry points before changing the barrier.

lessons.title: Outdoor sanitation still matters
lessons.summary: Tools, footwear, hands, plant debris and volunteer host plants can move pests and pathogens between garden zones.
lessons.cultivation: Being outdoors does not make biosecurity irrelevant; it changes the number of uncontrolled sources.
lessons.observe: Separate clean and suspect work, remove diseased debris appropriately and inspect new plants before moving them into the crop.

lessons.title: Separate biotic damage from weather and nutrition stress
lessons.summary: Wind abrasion, sunscald, hail, drought, waterlogging and nutrient symptoms can resemble pest or disease injury.
lessons.cultivation: Treating an abiotic problem as an insect or pathogen wastes time and can add unnecessary inputs.
lessons.observe: Use lesion pattern, distribution, pest signs, weather history, root-zone status and progression over time before choosing a cause.

knowledgeChecks: Why should scouting be systematic rather than symptom-triggered?
What evidence should be collected before choosing a wildlife barrier?

chapters.title: Pollen Drift, Sex Expression & Neighbor Risk
chapters.objective: Manage pollen as a landscape-scale, weather-dependent risk and inspect plants early enough for removal or containment decisions.

lessons.title: Cannabis pollen is windborne and distance-dependent
lessons.summary: Hemp/cannabis pollen concentration and deposition generally decline with distance from a source, but atmospheric transport can create a long tail beyond the nearest field edge.
lessons.cultivation: There is no single isolation radius that guarantees zero pollen exposure under all weather and terrain conditions.
lessons.observe: Identify nearby potential sources and record prevailing winds and flowering periods rather than relying only on straight-line distance.

lessons.title: Weather changes pollen movement
lessons.summary: Wind speed/direction, turbulence, atmospheric stability, humidity and timing of pollen release influence transport and deposition.
lessons.cultivation: A neighboring source can present different risk on different days even at the same distance.
lessons.observe: Use local wind records and field observations during the pollen-release window to update the risk assessment.

lessons.title: Scout sex expression before pollen release
lessons.summary: Regular or unexpected male/intersex flowers can release pollen within the crop; early identification is more useful than discovering seeded flowers later.
lessons.cultivation: Sex management is a repeated inspection task because expression can appear at different nodes and times.
lessons.observe: Inspect preflowers and reproductive sites on a schedule and document plant identity before any removal decision.

lessons.title: Neighbor communication and records reduce surprises
lessons.summary: For breeding or seedless production, neighboring cultivation plans and your own source records can matter as much as on-site plant selection.
lessons.cultivation: Unexpected seed set should be investigated from both internal and external pollen possibilities.
lessons.observe: Record internal male/intersex findings, nearby known sources, dates, wind events and where seed set appears in the canopy.

chapters.title: Seasonal Planning, Microclimates & Records
chapters.objective: Plan for site-specific weather transitions and convert each season into data for the next one.

lessons.title: The field contains multiple microclimates
lessons.summary: Slope, elevation, soil moisture, windbreaks, walls, tree lines and structures can create temperature, humidity, wind and frost differences within one property.
lessons.cultivation: A single weather station may miss the coldest low spot, windiest edge or slowest-drying flower zone.
lessons.observe: Place temporary sensors or repeat observations at suspected extremes and map them to crop position.

lessons.title: Build contingency triggers before severe weather
lessons.summary: Define actions for frost, extreme heat, high wind, prolonged rain, smoke/dust or irrigation failure before the event is already occurring.
lessons.cultivation: Preplanned thresholds and responsibilities reduce rushed decisions and help avoid damaging last-minute changes.
lessons.observe: Write the trigger, action, responsible person, stop condition and post-event inspection for each major site risk.

lessons.title: Photoperiod and seasonal timing interact with genotype
lessons.summary: Outdoor flowering response depends on genetics and local day length, while temperature and weather determine whether the resulting flowering window is practical.
lessons.cultivation: A genotype that flowers acceptably in one latitude or season may finish too late or encounter a wetter disease window elsewhere.
lessons.observe: Record first preflower, flowering onset, major developmental stages and local day length/weather for each genotype.

lessons.title: Close the season with a structured review
lessons.summary: Compare genotype performance, yield/quality observations, disease events, irrigation demand, support failures, harvest timing and weather using the same site map and batch IDs.
lessons.cultivation: The most valuable outdoor calendar is often the one built from several seasons of local observations rather than a generic national chart.
lessons.observe: Preserve raw weather/sensor data, photos and event dates, then write bounded conclusions and specific changes to test next season.
